lessons.title: Case Study: One Indian D2C Startup From a ₹2 Crore Seed to a ₹20 Crore Series A

children.text: Everything in this course happens to one company at once, so here is one company. Kesar and Co is an illustrative Jaipur brand selling ayurvedic haircare on its own website and on marketplaces, built by Ira, who runs product and operations, and Dhruv, who runs growth. The numbers are invented but internally consistent, and every decision below maps to a lesson you have already worked through. Follow it from ₹18 lakh of savings to a ₹20 crore Series A, and watch what the arithmetic does to everyone on the cap table.

body.text: A funding journey is not a series of announcements. It is one long argument with your own numbers, settled in public every 18 months when somebody prices what you have proved.

body.title: Kesar and Co, month 0 to month 46

events.title: Bootstrapped with ₹18 lakh
events.description: Ira and Dhruv incorporate a private limited company with 10,00,000 shares, split 60:40. They sign a founders' agreement with four-year vesting and a one-year cliff, and assign all IP to the company, including work done by the freelance designer who built the site.

events.title: ₹50 lakh angel cheque on a convertible
events.description: A Delhi angel who ran a personal care distribution business invests ₹50 lakh on an iSAFE with a ₹6 crore valuation cap and a 20% discount. No valuation is agreed, and the round closes in three weeks.

events.title: Seed round: ₹2 crore at ₹10 crore post-money
events.description: Revenue is ₹9 lakh a month. A seed fund invests ₹2 crore for 20%, an 8% ESOP pool is created pre-money, and the angel's note converts at its ₹6 crore cap.

events.title: The unit economics problem
events.description: Growth is real but every order loses money after acquisition costs. The founders stop spending on new customer acquisition in the worst-performing pin codes, push prepaid orders and rebuild the repeat purchase journey.

events.title: ₹1.2 crore bridge
events.description: Growth is on track but the Series A bar is still eight months away. The seed fund provides a bridge on a note carrying a 20% discount to the next round, sized to reach a defined revenue milestone with a margin.

events.title: Series A: ₹20 crore at ₹100 crore post-money
events.description: Revenue is ₹1.6 crore a month. A consumer-focused fund invests ₹20 crore for 20%, the ESOP pool is topped up by 4% pre-money, and the bridge note converts at its discount.

children.text: What Changed Between Seed and Series A

body.caption: The metrics that moved, month 22 to month 46

cells: About 12.7% growth a month, sustained for two years
Better sourcing, lighter packaging, fewer returns
Rose, which is normal as spend scales
The single biggest driver of the turnaround
Pin code targeting and address verification
Proof the brand was not renting customers from ad platforms

body.title: Monthly revenue, month 22 to month 46 (₹ lakh)

body.text: Look at months 26 to 30, where the line almost flattens. That is the period the founders spent fixing repeat purchase and returns instead of buying growth. It looks like lost time on a chart and it is the reason the Series A happened, because it turned a business that lost money per customer into one that made money per customer.

children.text: The Unit Economics Repair, in Numbers

stats.label: At seed
stats.context: ₹750 × 38% × 1.9 orders. A ratio of 1.04, which does not scale

stats.label: What did it
stats.context: Orders per customer rose from 1.9 to 3.2

stats.label: What it unlocked
stats.context: Growth an investor could pour money into without funding losses

body.title: Check the compounding
body.prompt: Kesar and Co grew from ₹9 lakh a month at seed to ₹160 lakh a month 24 months later. What average monthly growth rate does that imply? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: The multiple is ₹160 lakh ÷ ₹9 lakh = about 17.8 times. Spread over 24 months, the rate is 17.8 to the power of 1 ÷ 24, minus 1, which is roughly 12.7% a month. Note how ordinary that sounds and how extreme the result is: sustained compounding is what separates a Series A company from a decent small business.

children.text: The Cap Table, Round by Round

cells: Seed fund (₹2 crore plus ₹1.2 crore bridge)

body.text: Two things to notice. The founders fell from 100% to 49.5% across two rounds and still hold a majority between them, which is a healthy outcome. And Ira's 29.7% of a ₹100 crore company is worth ₹29.7 crore on paper, against 60% of a company worth almost nothing at month 0. Percentage down, value up, exactly as Lesson 1.2 promised.

body.title: What the angel's ₹50 lakh actually did

children.text: The angel invested at month 10 on a note with a ₹6 crore cap, when the company had 10,00,000 shares. That set a conversion price of ₹60 a share, so ₹50 lakh converted into roughly 83,000 shares at the seed round.

Compare that with converting at the seed price instead. The seed round valued the company at ₹10 crore post-money, so without the cap the same ₹50 lakh would have bought a materially smaller stake. The cap is what turned an early cheque into 5.5% of the company at seed, which after further dilution is 4.1% at Series A, worth ₹4.1 crore on ₹50 lakh invested.

Was that a bad deal for the founders? No. The angel came in when the company had almost no revenue, introduced them to two contract manufacturers and their first marketplace account manager, and took a risk nobody else would. The lesson from Lesson 3.3 still holds: the cap is a valuation agreed before you know what the company is worth, so model it before signing rather than being surprised at conversion.

body.title: What did the first cheque return?
body.prompt: The angel invested ₹50 lakh and holds 4.1% of the company at the ₹100 crore post-money Series A valuation. What multiple is that on the original investment? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 4.1% × ₹100 crore = ₹4.1 crore, against ₹50 lakh invested, which is about 8.2 times in roughly three years. On paper: the angel cannot sell these shares on NSE, and will realise the gain only in a secondary sale, a buyback or an exit.

body.caption: Six choices, and where each one appears in this course

cells: Four-year vesting with a one-year cliff, signed at incorporation, plus IP assignment from the freelance designer
Took ₹10 crore post-money when ₹16 crore was available from another investor with a 15% pool
Paused acquisition spend for four months to repair repeat purchase and returns
Reported the flat months and the fix, which is why the bridge conversation took nine days
A bridge tied to a milestone
₹1.2 crore sized to reach a defined revenue level with a margin, not a general extension
Accepted the valuation, pushed for 1x non-participating preference and broad-based weighted average anti-dilution

body.label: The counterfactual that matters most
body.value: The ₹16 crore seed they turned down
body.context: A second seed offer valued them at ₹16 crore post-money with a 15% pre-money ESOP pool and a 2x participating preference. Higher headline, worse ownership, and a bar their month-46 numbers would have struggled to clear. Taking ₹10 crore made the Series A a clean step up instead of a fight.

body.title: What actually unlocked the Series A?
body.question: Which change between month 22 and month 46 mattered most to the Series A investor?
options: Monthly revenue rising from ₹9 lakh to ₹1.6 crore
Orders per customer rising from 1.9 to 3.2, which turned a ratio of 1.04 into 2.3
Average order value rising from ₹750 to ₹920
The founders keeping a combined majority of 49.5%
body.explanation: Revenue growth is the headline, but it was fundable only because each customer became profitable. A company growing fast at a ratio of 1.04 is asking an investor to fund losses at scale. Rising order value helped, and founder ownership matters to the founders more than to the investor.

body.title: Rerun the story with a higher seed valuation
body.scenario: Suppose Ira and Dhruv had taken the other seed offer at month 22: ₹2 crore at ₹16 crore post-money, so 12.5% sold, with a 15% ESOP pool created pre-money and a 2x participating liquidation preference. Everything else about the business unfolds identically, and at month 46 the company is worth the same ₹100 crore on its fundamentals.
body.prompt: How would that decision have changed the Series A, the ownership and the founders' outcome?
body.modelAnswer:
Three effects, and only one of them is good for the founders.
1. Ownership at seed. The investor takes 12.5% instead of 20%, which sounds better, but the 15% pre-money pool instead of 8% takes 7 percentage points more out of the existing holders. Net of both, the founders and angel end up owning roughly the same or slightly less than under the ₹10 crore offer, while the investor owns less. The headline gain largely disappears into the pool.
2. The bar for the next round. A ₹16 crore post-money seed means the Series A must be priced comfortably above it, which at month 46 it still is, so this alone is survivable. The risk is the path: had the repeat purchase fix taken two extra quarters, a ₹16 crore seed would have made a flat or down round far more likely, and a down round would trigger anti-dilution for the seed investor and damage morale.
3. The preference, which is the real cost. A 2x participating preference on ₹2 crore means the seed fund takes ₹4 crore off the top of any exit and then also shares the remainder by percentage. In a ₹100 crore exit that costs the other shareholders several crore. In a mediocre exit, say ₹30 crore, it is devastating: ₹4 crore off the top plus a percentage share, from a pot that has to cover a Series A preference too.
Conclusion: they were right to take the lower valuation. A modest price with clean terms and a small pool beat a 60% higher headline with a big pool and a punitive preference, which is exactly the trade Lessons 3.2, 3.4 and 4.2 were arguing for.

body.title: The course in one checklist
steps: Raise only when money buys growth the business cannot buy on its own, and start with 9 to 12 months of runway left.
Match the cheque to the source: angels and micro VCs for small rounds, institutional funds for Series A.
Know your model's metrics, and measure LTV on contribution rather than revenue.
Incorporate properly, sign vesting and IP assignments early, and keep the cap table reconciled to your filings.
Compare offers on price per share and founder ownership after the pool, never on the headline valuation.
Negotiate preference and anti-dilution before valuation, because they decide the outcomes that actually happen.
Run a compressed process so decisions cluster, and find a lead investor rather than collecting followers.
Prepare the data room before signing a term sheet, and disclose every problem before diligence finds it.
After the round, set a burn ceiling, send honest monthly updates and write the trigger plan before you need it.
Plan backwards from the next round, and act at month 6 when the gap between plan and reality is still small.

body.title: The pattern underneath the whole journey
body.textWithBlank: Across both rounds the founders' percentage fell while the value of their holding rose, because dilution at a higher price per share makes your slice smaller and the ___ bigger.
body.explanation: Ira went from 60% of a company worth almost nothing to 29.7% of a company valued at ₹100 crore. Dilution only hurts when it happens at a flat or falling price, which is why over-pricing an early round is more dangerous than it looks.

cards.definition: Funding buys speed for a business that already works. It cannot manufacture demand that is not there.
Seed rounds are sold on conviction, Series A rounds on data that survives diligence.
Fix the profit per customer before scaling spend, or funding simply enlarges the loss.
Pool size, preference and anti-dilution routinely matter more than the valuation number.
12.7% a month for 24 months turned ₹9 lakh into ₹1.6 crore of monthly revenue.
Monthly updates that include the bad months are what make a bridge take nine days instead of nine weeks.
60% of nothing is worth less than 29.7% of ₹100 crore, provided each round is priced higher than the last.

points: Kesar and Co went from ₹18 lakh of founder savings to a ₹20 crore Series A in 46 months, through an angel note, a seed round and a bridge.
The founders fell from 100% to 49.5% combined, and Ira's stake went from 60% of almost nothing to 29.7% of ₹100 crore.
The Series A was unlocked by unit economics, not revenue: orders per customer rose from 1.9 to 3.2, taking the LTV to CAC ratio from 1.04 to 2.3.
Four flat-looking months spent fixing returns and repeat purchase were the most valuable months in the journey.
The angel's ₹6 crore cap turned ₹50 lakh into 4.1% worth ₹4.1 crore, which is why caps must be modelled before signing.
Turning down a ₹16 crore seed with a 15% pool and a 2x participating preference was the right call, because terms outlast headlines.
The bridge worked because it was tied to a defined milestone and because the investors had been told the truth every month.
Every rupee raised was priced against evidence. Build the evidence first, and the funding conversation becomes much shorter.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Kesar and Co, Ira, Dhruv and the angel are fictional, and every figure is illustrative and simplified: real rounds involve share-level arithmetic, negotiated terms, taxes and compliance steps covered earlier in this course. Percentages are rounded and may not sum exactly. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
